notes.b: Good equipment makes cooking easier and safer, but only if it suits the job. Choose for the quantity of food, the cooking method, the type of hob, durability, ease of cleaning and cost, and check how the material conducts heat (passes heat through it).
points: Buy equipment you will use often and can store easily, because a gadget used once a year wastes money and cupboard space.
A heavy, flat, thick base spreads heat evenly and reduces hot spots that scorch food and make it stick; a thin base heats unevenly.
Aluminium and copper conduct heat quickly and evenly, so they respond fast when the heat changes.
Stainless steel is durable and does not react with acidic foods, but it conducts heat less well, so good pans have a base bonded to copper or aluminium. It is not the best conductor.
Cast iron retains heat well and suits slow, even cooking such as braising, but it is heavy and rusts if left damp. Glass and ceramic dishes suit oven cooking and conduct heat slowly.
A non-stick coating allows frying with little fat, but it is scratched by metal utensils and damaged by overheating, for example heating an empty pan.
A close-fitting lid retains steam, so food simmers with less energy and in less time. The pan base should match the ring size, so that the full base makes contact with the heat source.
Induction hobs heat the pan by magnetism, so they need a pan with a magnetic (ferrous) base; aluminium and copper pans without one will not heat.
Handles should be firm, heat-resistant and fixed securely; plastic and wooden handles are not suitable for the oven unless the manufacturer states it.
notes.tip: Questions ask for features to look for when choosing a saucepan, frying pan or set of equipment. Cover base, material, lid, handle, size, cost and ease of cleaning, and don't call stainless steel the best conductor or say non-stick is safe at any temperature.

notes.h: A basic kitchen kit and accurate measuring
notes.b: A practical kitchen needs a core set of tools, and recipes only work if ingredients are measured accurately.
points: Pans and dishes: saucepans of different sizes, a frying pan, a roasting tin, a casserole, and baking tins and trays.
Preparation tools: mixing bowls, a sieve, a colander, wooden spoons, a spatula, a whisk, a grater, a rolling pin, a peeler and a tin opener.
Measuring and checking tools: a measuring jug, scales, measuring spoons, a timer and a thermometer.
Weigh and measure accurately with scales, jugs and spoons, because too much or too little of an ingredient can change how a dish turns out.
Ingredients are measured in metric, and spoon measures are level, not heaped, so that every cook gets the same amount.
notes.tip: Coursework asks you to name the equipment for a dish and say why it was chosen. Pair each item with its job.

notes.b: Knives are the most dangerous everyday tool in the kitchen, so choosing the right one and handling it correctly prevents most cuts. Chopping boards need care too, because they can pass germs between foods.
points: A cook's knife is used for general chopping, a paring knife for small, detailed work and peeling, a serrated (bread) knife for bread and soft-skinned foods, and a carving knife for carving cooked meat.
A sharp knife is safer than a blunt one because it cuts with less force and is less likely to slip.
The claw grip curls the fingertips of the guiding hand under, so the knuckles guide the blade and the fingertips stay clear of it.
Place the chopping board on a damp cloth or non-slip mat so that it cannot move while cutting.
Colour-coded boards (for raw meat, fish, vegetables and cooked foods) keep them apart, preventing cross-contamination (germs spreading from raw to ready-to-eat food).
Wash boards well after raw meat, and replace badly scored boards because germs can lodge in the cuts.
Carry a knife by its handle with the blade pointing down and away from the body; never leave a knife in a sink of washing-up water, where it cannot be seen.
Store knives in a block, on a rack or on a magnetic strip, so that the edges are protected and the blades are not loose in a drawer.
notes.tip: Questions ask for three safety guidelines for using a knife. Choose from sharp knife, claw grip, steady board, carrying blade down, and never leaving knives in washing-up water.

notes.h: Safe use of the hob, oven and electrical appliances
notes.b: Most kitchen accidents are burns, scalds, cuts and electric shocks, and most are avoidable with a few habits. Each habit below removes a specific danger.
points: Hob: turn pan handles inwards over the hob so they cannot be knocked or pulled, use a ring that matches the pan size, and never leave hot oil or fat unattended.
Keep tea towels and flexes away from the hob, where they can catch fire or melt.
Lift lids away from the face so that escaping steam does not scald.
Oven: place the shelves before heating, open the door carefully, and use a stable tray for hot dishes.
Use dry oven gloves or a dry cloth to handle hot dishes; a damp cloth conducts heat and causes scalds.
Electrical: keep the flex of appliances away from hot surfaces and water, never handle an appliance with wet hands, and don't overload sockets.
Switch off and unplug an appliance before cleaning its blades or removing food from them, and do not use one with a damaged flex or plug; it must be repaired or replaced before use.

Pressure cooker: check that the sealing ring and valve are clean and undamaged, never force the lid, and open it only after the pressure has fallen. Microwave: use microwave-safe containers, never put metal in the cavity, and cover and stir food.
notes.tip: Questions ask for three safety guidelines for using the hob, oven, knife or an electrical appliance. Give three distinct, specific rules, each with its reason.

notes.b: Beyond individual appliances, a few habits keep the whole kitchen safe, especially when something goes wrong.
points: Clean up spills at once, because a wet or greasy floor causes slips and falls.
Keep a fire blanket in the kitchen and know how to use it, so a small pan fire can be smothered quickly.
Never use water on a fat fire, because it causes the burning fat to flare up and spread.
notes.tip: Safety points count in coursework evaluation of a practical dish. Be ready to say what you did to work safely and why.

notes.b: Looking after equipment makes it last longer and keeps food safe. The right care depends on the material, so follow the manufacturer's care instructions.
points: Wash equipment in hot soapy water or in a dishwasher, then rinse, dry thoroughly and store it clean and dry, so that bacteria cannot grow and metal does not rust.
Do not run cold water into a hot pan; the sudden change in temperature can warp the base and crack a non-stick or ceramic surface. Soak burnt pans before scrubbing.
Cast iron must be dried straight after washing and wiped with a thin film of oil to prevent rust.
Use wooden or silicone utensils on non-stick surfaces, whereas metal utensils scratch them.
Use abrasive pads only on surfaces that tolerate them; stainless steel and cast iron tolerate them better than non-stick coatings.
Wooden items are not left to soak, because the wood absorbs water.
Dishcloths, sponges, tea towels and brushes can carry bacteria and should be changed or washed regularly.
Store knives safely, and stack pans with protection between them so non-stick surfaces are not scratched.
notes.tip: Questions ask for three guidelines for cleaning non-stick pans. Use: no metal tools, no harsh abrasives, no overheating, and no cold water into a hot pan.

notes.b: In the practical coursework, equipment is part of what you are marked on, because it shows you can plan and work like a competent cook.
points: Area B assignments ask you to describe new equipment or a new skill, and the planning section lists the key equipment you will use.
You should be able to name the equipment for a dish, say why it was chosen, and explain how it was used safely and hygienically.
notes.tip: Safety points in planning and carrying out a practical dish are asked about in coursework evaluation.

keyTerms.definition: The transfer of bacteria from raw food, hands or equipment to food that is ready to eat.
A knife-handling technique in which the fingertips of the guiding hand are curled under so that the knuckles guide the blade.
A pan with a thick base that spreads heat evenly across the cooking surface and reduces hot spots.
A surface on a pan that prevents food sticking, allowing cooking with little fat, but damaged by overheating and metal utensils.
A heavy metal used for cookware that retains heat well and must be dried and oiled to prevent rust.
A knife with a toothed edge used for cutting bread and soft-skinned foods.
A sealed pan that cooks food quickly under steam pressure and must not be opened until the pressure is released.
Describes a container marked as suitable for microwave use and containing no metal.
A hob that heats magnetic pans directly through electromagnetic induction, so only pans with a magnetic base can be used.

factCards.term: Three knife types for kitchen use
factCards.definition: Cook's knife for general chopping; serrated knife for bread and soft-skinned foods; paring knife for small, detailed work.

factCards.term: Three rules for carrying a knife
factCards.definition: Point the blade down and away from the body; carry it by the handle at the side; never try to catch a falling knife.

factCards.term: Four ways to prevent cross-contamination in the kitchen
factCards.definition: Use separate colour-coded chopping boards for raw and cooked foods; wash hands after handling raw meat; store raw meat below ready-to-eat food in the fridge; clean and sanitise equipment between tasks.

factCards.term: Three care rules for cast iron
factCards.definition: Dry it straight after washing; wipe it with a thin film of oil; never leave it soaking or damp.

factCards.term: Two things that damage a non-stick coating
factCards.definition: Overheating an empty pan, and scraping the surface with metal utensils.

factCards.term: Two checks before using a pressure cooker
factCards.definition: That the sealing ring and the valve are clean and undamaged; that the lid is locked on correctly before heating.

questions.prompt: Outline three factors to consider when selecting a saucepan for use on an induction hob.
questions.model: Base material: the pan must have a magnetic base, otherwise it will not heat on an induction hob. Base thickness: a heavy, thick base spreads heat evenly and reduces hot spots. Size: the pan base should match the ring size so that the full base makes contact with the hob. A close-fitting lid retains steam and reduces cooking time and energy. Heat-resistant handles that are firmly fixed make the pan safe to lift and move.

questions.prompt: Explain how a non-stick frying pan and a wooden chopping board should be used and cared for so that they stay safe and hygienic.
questions.model: Non-stick pan: avoid overheating an empty pan, as this damages the coating. Use wooden or silicone utensils, because metal scratches the surface. Allow the pan to cool before washing it, since cold water on a hot pan can warp the base or crack the coating. Wash in hot soapy water, rinse and dry before storing. Chopping board: place it on a damp cloth or non-slip mat so it does not move while cutting. Keep it separate from raw meat and ready-to-eat foods, using a colour-coded board for each. Wash in hot soapy water after each use, dry thoroughly and store upright so air can circulate. Replace boards that become deeply cut or grooved, because bacteria can collect in the cuts.
